drills.q: You have 40 confirmed anomaly labels out of 2 million records. Do you train a supervised classifier on them?
drills.a: Generally no -- 40 positive examples is usually too few to train a reliable discriminative classifier, especially if the anomaly type might evolve. Better to use semi-supervised/unsupervised detection methods and use those 40 labels for threshold calibration and evaluation instead of classifier training data.

drills.q: A fraud model reports 99.8% accuracy at a 0.2% true fraud rate. Is this a good result?
drills.a: Not necessarily meaningful at all -- a model that predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction would score 99.8% accuracy while catching zero fraud. Accuracy is useless here; check PR-AUC and precision/recall at the actual operating threshold instead.

drills.q: An IsolationForest model is flagging 30% of all records as anomalies, which the team knows is far too many. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
drills.a: The contamination parameter is set too high (or left at a default/guess that doesn't match the real anomaly rate), directly shifting the decision threshold. Set contamination from a validated estimate of the true anomaly rate and re-validate periodically.

drills.q: A OneClassSVM model trained with default parameters never flags anything as anomalous. Diagnose.
drills.a: nu is likely left at its default of 0.5, which assumes roughly 50% of training data is contamination -- an assumption wildly wrong for a real anomaly rate under 1-5%. This produces a decision boundary calibrated to the wrong assumption. Set nu near the actual expected anomaly rate.

drills.q: A fraud detection system has 1,000,000 legitimate transactions and 1,000 fraudulent ones. A model has a 1% false positive rate. Compute the absolute number of false alarms and explain why ROC-AUC won't reflect how bad this is.
drills.a: 1% of 1,000,000 = 10,000 false alarms -- 10x the actual fraud count. ROC-AUC's false positive rate is computed relative to the huge true-negative count (999,000), so a 1% FPR barely moves ROC-AUC even though the absolute false-positive volume swamps the true fraud count and makes the alert queue operationally unusable.

drills.q: An autoencoder-based anomaly detector worked well for a month after launch, then false positives suddenly spiked. What's the most likely cause and what should have been in place to prevent it?
drills.a: The underlying 'normal' distribution drifted (seasonality, product change, evolving behavior) and the reconstruction-error threshold, computed once at launch, is now miscalibrated against current normal behavior. A periodic threshold recalibration process against a recent known-clean window should have been in place.

drills.q: A team wants to use a deep autoencoder for fraud detection on a dataset with only 12 tabular features. Push back with the tradeoff.
drills.a: On 12 tabular features, Isolation Forest or LOF will very likely match the autoencoder's detection quality at a fraction of the engineering cost -- no architecture design, training stability concerns, or non-trivial reconstruction-error threshold calibration to solve. 'More complex model' doesn't imply 'more accurate model' on simple, low-dimensional tabular data.

drills.q: Design the end-to-end production pipeline for a manufacturing defect detection system, from raw sensor signal to a final human decision, including the piece most systems skip.
drills.a: Feature/signal pipeline -> scoring model -> raw anomaly score -> threshold tuned against real cost tradeoff (missed defect vs false-alarm inspection cost) -> alert routes to human inspection queue -> inspector confirms/rejects -> that label feeds periodic retraining. The piece most systems skip is the feedback loop from confirmed/rejected labels back into retraining -- without it the model can't adapt as the true defect distribution drifts.

drills.q: Your anomaly detection system has run for 8 months with no retraining and performance is degrading. Feature distributions look stable when compared against the training snapshot. What's your next hypothesis?
drills.a: The anomaly TYPE itself has evolved rather than the baseline normal distribution -- fraud patterns, intrusion techniques, and defect modes often adapt specifically because they're adversarial or upstream processes changed in ways not captured by current features. This points toward needing new features or an expanded label set from recent confirmed cases, not just threshold recalibration.

drills.q: You compare Isolation Forest and an autoencoder on a labeled evaluation set of only 30 confirmed historical anomalies, and the autoencoder shows a slightly higher PR-AUC. Should you deploy the autoencoder?
drills.a: Be cautious -- PR-AUC computed from only 30 positive examples has high variance, and a marginal difference could easily be noise. Bootstrap the comparison or report confidence intervals, and weight the decision toward the simpler, more maintainable model (Isolation Forest) unless the more complex option shows a meaningful, not marginal, improvement.

drills.q: A LOF-based fraud system is missing a fraud pattern the team knows is real: transactions that are extremely large in absolute terms but happen to sit near other large-transaction accounts. Why does LOF miss this, and what fixes it?
drills.a: LOF measures density relative to a point's LOCAL neighborhood -- if the fraudulent large transactions sit near other legitimately large-transaction accounts, they look locally normal even though they're a clear GLOBAL outlier. Combine LOF with a global method (Isolation Forest, z-score/IQR) since no single anomaly definition covers both local and global cases.
